body.text: Dera, being a Punjabi, Sindhi, Dogri, Kutchi, Saraiki, and Gujarati word, draws its etymological lineage from the Persian word derah or dirah, with variations such as dehra, dero, daro, dhoro, dahar. It can be called a camp, residence, or the abode of a charismatic person, variously called baba, guru, swami, pir, murshid, bhagat, sadhu, sant, or monk, who is considered to be an embodiment of high moral values and spiritual attributes. It is around such an enamouring personality that the core identity of a dera is constructed. Free from the moral and authoritative bindings of mainstream religious rituals and ceremonies, where people belonging to different faiths, regions, languages, castes, and classes converge to seek the blessings of their spiritual mentors and look for solutions to their day-to-day problems, deras resemble akharas, ashrams, gufas, dargahs, khanqahs, jama’at khanas, matths, takiyas, tillas, and various other down-to-earth devotional spaces.

Though often equated with gurdwaras, temples, sects, and cults, deras are distinguishable from all of them in terms of architectural designs, beliefs, and practices. For instance, gurdwaras are religious centres where only the Shri Guru Granth Sahib—the central holy scripture of the Sikh faith—is revered as the eternal Guru; no other religious scriptures are recited. Worship of idols and human gurus, common rituals in temples, sects, and cults, find no place in gurdwaras.

A motley of various sacred scriptures is recited in deras, which differ from both sects and cults. Sects and cults are derivatives/subsets of mainstream religious orders, though they follow their own distinct beliefs, ceremonies, traditions, and practices. In some respects, deras resemble cults: they are quasi-religious groups headed by charismatic persons, mostly males, with distinct and unorthodox ideologies, rituals, and practices and either directly, or through authorised representatives, reveal “holy-naam” (a purportedly spiritually-charged word considered as priceless spiritual wealth) to their designated followers during meticulously planned and thoroughly guarded initiation ceremonies.

Deras are alternative sociocultural and syncretic religious spaces mostly frequented by socially deprived and economically poor sections whom they tend to motivate by offering hope for a better future, particularly in the face of a fast-receding welfare state. By extending much-needed social, spiritual, and moral support to the downtrodden, deras promise to make a significant difference to their lives. Within the sprawling premises of deras, the downtrodden find a welcoming place—what Nancy Fraser called “subaltern counter-public”—endowed with an egalitarian social episteme free from the afflictions of caste discriminations, social exclusion, and the subtle indignities often faced by them within mainstream religious spheres. Thus deras may be seen as potent agents of social mobility and syncretic religious realms for the emancipation and empowerment of socially deprived and economically marginalised sections.

Some deras have acquired cult-like structures with their own charitable hospitals, educational institutions, technical training centres, local transport systems, gas stations, provision stores, huge pillar-free air-conditioned satsang (congregation) halls, digital media, weekly magazines, and libraries. Such meticulously curated and widespread institutional set-ups foster networks of dense reciprocal social and religious relations between the “babas” and their followers. Well-planned routine darshan (face-to-face interactions) programmes between babas and devotees are used to forge and reinforce reciprocity and mutual trustworthiness.

A large number of followers, including notable political personalities, regularly gather at such monthly/annual satsangs/samagams (religious congregations) organised by deras, especially on the anniversaries (jayanti) of their babas. On such occasions, politicians across party lines indulge in photo diplomacy to showcase their intimacy with the babas; it helps to secure an edge over political adversaries in elections.

The social legitimacy that deras acquire through their welfare programmes eventually translates into a viable political agency based on an informal alliance between babas and political plutocrats. The babas garner the electoral support of their followers for their politician friends. The strategy is to deflect popular attention from material miseries and destroy the will for change in the name of piety, thrift, and simple living. “How long shall the state continue to fiddle with the rule of law to flatter the babas and their followers?” said Pramod Kumar in a 2017 article in Times of India.

Deras initially started out as modest and local centres of alternative and syncretic religious spaces. As they grew in popularity and social influence, some of them even had villages, cities, towns, and districts named after them.
The first wave

The origin of deras in Punjab can be traced to medieval times. Patterned on viharas and sangharams (temples and monasteries) of Jainism and Buddhism, constructed over centuries under royal patronage, the first deras came up with the emergence of the Nath Sampradaya founded by the yogi Matsyendranath in the 10th century. Drawing on Buddhist, Shaivite, Vedantic, and Yoga traditions, the Nath Sampradaya expanded into 12 panths (branches), which in turn established a large number of Gorakhnathi deras in different parts of India under the stewardship of Yogi Gorakhnath, the legendary disciple of Matsyendranath.

The deras of the Nath Sampradaya were called shrines/monasteries/Nath-warah/akharas. Their headquarters were “Tilla Yogian” in Jhelum district of undivided Punjab. Baba Nanak is said to have visited Tilla Yogian and mentioned the names of Matsyendranath, Gorakhnath, and Charpatnath in his sacred verses. Like present-day deras, the Nath Sampradaya deras were open to all, irrespective of caste, class, and creed.
The second wave

In the next phase were Sufi deras that emerged during the Sultanate in north-western India in the 13th century. Popularly known as khanqahs and jama’at khanas, these were of 12 silsilahs/tariqahs (schools/orders), the Chishtiyyah and Suhrawardiyya being the most famous. These deras began emerging with the founding of the Chishtiyyah silsilah by the Sufi sant Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti of Sistan, who established his dera, Ajmer Sharif Dargah, in Ajmer, Rajasthan, in 1236.
Chishtiyyah deras multiplied during the time of Baba Farid (1173/1175‐1266), whose sacred verses are included in the Guru Granth Sahib.

The Suhrawardiyya silsilah played a significant role in the formation of Sufi derasin Punjab. Unlike the Chishtiyyah order, the Suhrawardi Sufis led a life of material comfort, like some of the babas of today’s deras. They also took an active interest in politics and were patronised by the rulers of their time who believed that association with the Sufi babas would bring prestige and social legitimacy because of the goodwill they enjoyed in society.

In the mid-15th century, Qadiriyyah, another Sufi silsilah, was founded by Shah Niamatullah and Makhdum Muhammed Jilan in Punjab. Syed Muhammad Ghons, Muhammad Fazol, Shah Latif Barri, Shah Husain, Shah Anayat, Bhuleh Shah, Sultan Bahu, and Mian Mir were among its most famous murshids who had their distinct deras. Mian Mir of Lahore of this silsilah laid the foundation stone of the Golden Temple of Amritsar.
In contemporary Punjab, the khanqah of Pir Buhdhu Shah in Batala, and Pir Abdula Shah in Mandhali (Phaghwara) are famous Sufi deras of the Qadiriyyah order.

Yet another famous silsilah of the Sufis in Punjab is the Naqshbandi order. In north-west India and undivided Punjab, its famous shrines were: Dargah Hazrat Sain Tawakkal Shah in Ambala, Dargah Shaikh Ahmad Faruqi (Mujaddid) in Sirhind, Dargah Saif-ud-Din Sirhandi Faruqi in Sirhind, Sayad Nur Muhammad in Sirhind, Sayad Imam Ali Shah in Gurdaspur, Mahmud Shah in Lahore, and Haji Muhammad Sayyid in Lahore.

Sufi orders and their deras became part of the social and spiritual life of the people, especially among marginalised sections, in Punjab. They carried enormous influence in society and in the Mughal court. After Akbar’s death, Shaikh Ahmad Faruqi (Mujaddid), the head of Naqshbandi Dargah in Sirhind, was able to manipulate Jahangir into folding up Dīn-i Ilāhī, the ethical and spiritual system introduced by Akbar, and to replace it with the Islamic Sharia. He is also believed to have influenced Jahangir to execute Guru Arjan Dev, fifth Sikh Guru, in 1606.
The third wave

The third phase of Punjab’s deras began during the early period of the Sikh Gurus. Soon after the passing away of Guru Baba Nanak (1539), the founder of the Sikh faith, his eldest son, Baba Sri Chand, established a separate and parallel seat of authority/cult/dera at Derha Baba Nanak. Dattu, the eldest son of Guru Angad, established his separate religious centre at Khadur, and Mohan, the eldest son of Guru Amar Das, followed suit at Goindwal.

This early tradition of Sikh deras, initiated by the unsuccessful attempts of the “fake” claimants to the title of Guru within the evolving mainstream of the Sikh faith, led to the formation of four more dissenter sects of mainstream Sikhism: Minas (scoundrels), also called Chhota Mel (lesser clan), followers of Prithi Chand, the eldest son of Guru Ram Dass, the fourth master; Dhirmallias, followers of Dhir Mall, eldest son of Gurditta, son of the sixth guru Hargobind; Ramraiyas, followers of Ram Rai; and Masandias, followers of Masands. Each of them established separate deras at different places: Minas at Hehar, a village near Lahore; Dhirmallians at Kartarpur; Ramraiyas in present-day Dehradun; and Masandias/Handalias/Niranjanias at Jandiala.

The 22 manjis (peripheral religious centres),each headed by a chosen Sikh called masand, established by Guru Amar Das, the third Guru, to propagate the faith and help distant followers to congregate and collect offerings, eventually metamorphosed into Sikh deras.

Subsequently, many more deras of varied nomenclatures appeared at different intervals. Among the most prominent of these were: Addan Sahi, Almast, Bala Hasna, Bandei Khalsa (Bandapanthis), Bhagat Bhagwaniye, Bhaktmalliye, Bhaktpanthi, Bindrabani Nanak Sahi, Divana, Gahir Gambharia, Gangu Sahia, Gulabdasi, Handali, Hiradasia, Jitmalliye, Mihanshahiye, Mahima Sahia, Namdhari/Kukas, Nanakpanthis, Nihang, Nirankari, Radhasoami, Ramdas Ka, Sacha Sauda, Sahajdhari, Sangat Sahibiye, Satinamia, Satkartaria, Sewapanthis, Suthrashahi, Singh Ji Mat, Udasi, and Vanjara.

Nirmalas (spotless) and the Gianis (conversant with sacred scriptures) constituted yet another early Sikh sant tradition, which also established its corresponding Sikh deras. Damdami Taksal (Jatha Bhindran-Mehta), located at Gurdwara Gurdarshan Parkash in Mehta, Amritsar, is the most prominent among them, currently headed by Baba Harnam Singh Khalsa (also known as Baba Harnam Singh Dhumma).

The Sikh dera wave intensified with the emergence of a popular rural Sikh sant tradition in early 20th century Punjab; impressive deras/gurdwaras were established in villages all over Punjab. Almost every village in Punjab has one or more such deras/gurdwaras built around the personal spiritual aura of a sant/baba. Some of the most frequently visited deras of the rural Sikh sant tradition are Bhucho Mandi, Dhadrian, Harkhowal, Harian Belan, Kaleran, Mastuana, Nanaksar, Rarewala, Ratwara, Reru Sahib, and Takhtupura. Many such deras reposed faith in the Shri Guru Granth Sahib. But some of them produced their own distinct and vast literature, which is considered kachibani (false) and any dealings with such literature were pronounced as punishable, as per the mainstream Sikh Rehat Maryada (code of conduct).
The fourth wave

The fourth wave of deras began with the emergence of separate deras associated with the lowest castes, mainly emboldened by the Ad Dharm movement of the 1920s, which tactically cashed in on the mass appeal of Guru Ravidass by using his pictures as its emblem, reciting his bani and narrating legends about him as illustrations of the power, pride, and glory of oppressed segments.

Since then, Ad Dharmis have organised themselves into various Guru Ravidass Sabhas (societies) and established a large number of Ravidass deras in India and abroad. According to a rough estimate, there are around 75 Ravidass deras overseas. In Indian Punjab, there are more than 9,000 Sikh and non-Sikh deras in the rural areas.

In addition to deras that emerged during different waves, there are some deras which claim to have arisen from non-denominational “social” or “spiritual” movements and are open to all—Dera Radhasoami Beas, DeraSach Khand Ballan, Divya Jyoti Jagarti Sansthan Noormahal, Dera Sacha Sauda, Sirsa, Dera Baba Murad Shah, Nakodar, Bhaniarawala Dera, Dera Baba Mast Ram Ji Ucha Jatana, and deras of Nirankaris and Namdharis.
Deras, neoliberalism, and electoral arithmetic

Deras seem to be acquiring wider currency in the era of the neoliberal market economy. Taken over by “bling babas” who dress themselves fabulously and equip their deras with state-of-the-art gadgets and facilities, deras help their adherents to reconstruct distinct socio-religious identities in the wake of shocks produced by neoliberal reforms. Given their wider social reach and moral acceptability, deras act as credible agencies for the convergence of elites and commoners, rich and poor, as well as reputed state functionaries and ordinary members of civil society. Close affinities between babas and their ardent followers, on the one hand, and between babas, politicians, and bureaucrats, on the other, at a time when the erstwhile welfare state is retreating, have expanded the social, political, and cultural reach of deras. The personal aura of the babas is also enhanced.

The neoliberal economic set-up has pushed back the possibility of redistribution of land. Instead of resolving the contradictions of caste and class, neoliberal market reforms have further deepened the divides caused by these. The state’s capacity to address discrimination against the lower castes and weaker sections by reducing inequality in social and economic domains is undermined. The neoliberal economic reforms were supposed to counteract the ever-increasing menace of fiscal crises and end chronic poverty. But, as cogently argued by Sunil Khilnani, that dream remains unrealised.

Chronic poverty, which is rooted in India’s hierarchical social order, has been further complicated by the widening gulf between the rich and the poor in the neoliberal economic regime. In an indirect way, this increases the scope of babas to expand their dera followings and, eventually, their positions in an electoral democracy.

This works as a chain reaction. The babas’ links with politicians and bureaucrats help them in securing favours for themselves and their followers. The deras become strengthened and politicians win strong support bases.

The deras nurture constituencies among marginalised sections by holding out the hope of a better future, which appears attractive in the context of discriminatory social hierarchies and a vanishing welfare state. Projected as safe heavens, deras offer solace from worldly sufferings. Caught between stiff competition for jobs in the private sector and dwindling opportunities in the public sector since the early 1990s, economically vulnerable sections have been turning to deras in large numbers. The deras, in turn, are able to provide social welfare benefits like basic healthcare and educational facilities.

In a country with poor social security and little comfort for “losers”, deras attract with their promise of community, spiritual purpose, and social amenities. They provide succour to those who were left to fend for themselves, offering services that in developed countries would be provided by professional service providers such as marriage counsellors, psychologists, and caregivers. This makes it possible to project the babas as “saviours” and “messengers of God”.
Refuge of subalterns

In a society where the boundaries between religion and politics are often blurred, the deras with their massive subaltern support base have become immensely powerful. Over the years, large numbers of upper caste and upper class people have also gravitated towards deras, seeking solutions for their social, spiritual, and domestic problems. Many people, especially women, flock to deras hoping the babas will cure their relatives of drug addiction and other socio-psychological ailments. Many people seek the assurance of the birth of a male child. Others ask for mehar (grace) to excel in their worldly endeavours or to succeed in their efforts to go abroad. There are deras where people offer toy aeroplanes as a token of their mannat (wish) to go abroad.
Many lower-caste members of the Indian diaspora take pride in making devotional visits to their respective deras, which have given them confidence, and created a kind of social capital for them.

It is commonly believed that deras impart moral strength to their followers and equip them to face the challenges of day-to-day life by building wide social networks and cultivating a sense of social cohesiveness. Deras counsel, eulogise, and sometimes even disparage political leaders across party lines. Close ties between babas of deras and political leaders often strengthen both sides.

Deras mediate between state and civil society, government officials and common people, and facilitate dialogues between different religious groups. Primarily based on the allegiance of historically excluded, marginalised, and poverty-stricken sections, deras have collectively emerged as a credible alternative to mainstream religions.

The persistence of discriminatory caste-based social structures, within the mundane boundaries of the so-called egalitarian domains of the mainstream religions, the erosion of the joint family, and the gradual but continuing withdrawal of the state from public welfare programmes are other factors that have helped the growth of deras.

Ronki Ram is Emeritus Professor, Institute for Development and Communication, Chandigarh. He was formerly the Shaheed Bhagat Singh Chair Professor and dean of the faculty of arts at the Panjab University, Chandigarh.
